entry.label: Organisational recursion
entry.description: A domain-specific use of recursion in which operational units may themselves be treated as viable systems with corresponding requirements at another level. Visual nesting alone is not enough.
entry.canonical_definition: A domain-specific use of recursion in which an organisational system contains operational units that may themselves be treated as systems with structurally corresponding viability requirements at another level.

profile.title: Organisational recursion
profile.canonical_definition: A domain-specific use of recursion in which an organisational system contains operational units that may themselves be treated as systems with structurally corresponding viability requirements at another level.
profile.summary: In the VSM tradition, a viable operational unit may itself contain operations and meta-systemic functions. The same broad viability requirements recur, while purpose, environment, scale and implementation differ at each level.
profile.why_it_matters: Organisations often centralise decisions that require local variety or mistake reporting lines for system levels. Recursion helps locate the system-in-focus and test whether each operational unit has sufficient autonomy and regulatory support.
key_distinctions: recursive viability vs repeated organisation chart
historical_lineage: Stafford Beer developed recursive viability within management cybernetics
Diagnosing the System for Organizations made the model operational
later VSM practice developed recursive mapping techniques
practice_connections: test whether operational units are genuinely viable or merely departments
avoid forcing one diagram onto every scale
common_misreadings: recursion means the same five departments at every level
one VSM diagram represents the whole organisation once and for all
open_checks: limits and critiques of recursive mapping
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.
